You type and format on this page the way you would in Word, with the </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t>ribbon</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> across the top of the window. Every pause, the document is compiled to PDF so you can see exactly what will be printed. Behind the scenes it is stored as a structured model (headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, equations) that is turned into clean, readable </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Courier New" w:hAnsi="Courier New"/></w:rPr><w:t>.tex</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> source on demand.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>This page is itself a KherveTeX document. Click anywhere in it and type, change a heading, or break something on purpose: nothing you do here is saved unless you save it, and the New button at the top left always gives you a fresh page.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>The ribbon</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>As in Word, the commands live on one ribbon, grouped by task. Click a tab name to bring its buttons forward:</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Home: the clipboard, fonts, bold and italic, lists, alignment and the Styles gallery.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Insert: page breaks, tables, figures, drawings, links, equations, theorems and chemistry.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Layout: margins, page size, one to three columns and the document type (article, thesis, journal class and so on).</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Examples: ready-made documents of every type, this tour, and your own templates.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>References: citations, footnotes, captions and cross-references.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Review: spelling, comments, and sharing with Overleaf.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Compile: compile now, auto-compile, and PDF output.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>History: snapshots and the version history.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>View: the page, the LaTeX code, the console and the PDF.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Help: the user guide, keyboard shortcuts and updates.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Click in a table, a picture or an equation and extra tabs (Table Design, Table Layout, Picture, Theorem, Equation) appear beside the others, as in Word. The small buttons on the left of the tab names save, open, print and undo; Compile PDF sits on the right. The menu bar above holds everything else (File, Edit, View, Insert, Format, Tools, Window, Help), and the switch at the bottom right of the window flips between the light and dark themes.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">3 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Quick start</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The shortest path from an empty page to a finished PDF:</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Press Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on a Mac) for a blank page, or pick a ready-made document from the Examples tab.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Choose the document type on the Layout tab, then type your title and text. The Styles gallery on the Home tab turns a paragraph into a heading, an abstract or a keyword line.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Add what you need from the Insert and References tabs: a table, an equation, a footnote, a citation, a cross-reference.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Watch the PDF beside the page (Ctrl+4), or press Compile PDF at the top right (Ctrl+Shift+C).</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Save with Ctrl+S. Export a PDF, a .tex file or a Word file from File > Export.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">4 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Views: page, code and PDF</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">The View tab shows the same document three ways. </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t>Visual</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> (Ctrl+1) is this page, where you write. </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t>Code</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> (Ctrl+2) shows the LaTeX that KherveTeX generates, so you can read it, copy it or learn from it. </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t>PDF</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> keeps the compiled result beside the page (Ctrl+4), and </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t>Detach PDF</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> moves it to its own window, for a second screen. Turn it off to write undisturbed.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">If something looks wrong in the PDF, the </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t>Console</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> button on the View tab lists the compiler messages in plain text.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">5 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Formatting text</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Select text and use the Font group on the Home tab to make it </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t>bold</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>italic</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:u w:val="single"/></w:rPr><w:t>underlined</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:strike/></w:rPr><w:t>struck through</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> or </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Courier New" w:hAnsi="Courier New"/></w:rPr><w:t>monospaced</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>. Subscripts (H</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:vertAlign w:val="subscript"/></w:rPr><w:t>2</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>O), superscripts (m</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:vertAlign w:val="superscript"/></w:rPr><w:t>2</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">) and </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:smallCaps/></w:rPr><w:t>small caps</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> work the same way. Every mark becomes the matching LaTeX command, so the PDF always agrees with the page.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">5.1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Headings and paragraph styles</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The Styles gallery on the Home tab turns the current paragraph into a heading (five levels, numbered automatically), a title, an author line, an abstract or a keyword line. Each tile is drawn in the font and size the document type prints it in. Alignment (left, centre, right, justified) sits in the Paragraph group beside it.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">5.2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Lists</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The list buttons in the Paragraph group start a bulleted or numbered list; items nest with Tab and Shift+Tab. Inside an item you can use bold, links, footnotes and inline math like any other text. Some things worth knowing:</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Use a bulleted list for things with no order, such as an inventory or a set of options.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Use a numbered list for a procedure, where the order matters.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Nested lists change their bullet style on their own at each depth.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">6 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Mathematics</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">The Equations group on the Insert tab holds it all. <w:document xmlns:wpc="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingCanvas" xmlns:mo="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/mac/office/2008/main" xmlns:mc="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/markup-compatibility/2006" xmlns:mv="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:mac:vml" xmlns:o="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:office" xmlns:r="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships" xmlns:m="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/math" xmlns:v="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:vml" xmlns:wp14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:wp="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:w10="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:word" xmlns:w="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/wordprocessingml/2006/main" xmlns:w14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordml" xmlns:wpg="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingGroup" xmlns:wpi="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingInk" xmlns:wne="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2006/wordml" xmlns:wps="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingShape" mc:Ignorable="w14 wp14"><w:body><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Title"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Thermal conductivity of boron nitride–epoxy composites</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Subtitle"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>A. Author¹, B. Coauthor¹, C. Reviewer²</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:vertAlign w:val="superscript"/></w:rPr><w:footnoteReference w:id="1"/></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="center"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>¹ Department of Materials Engineering, Northfield University</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="center"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>² Halden Institute of Applied Physics</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="center"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:i w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t>a.author@example.org</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>Epoxy resins are good electrical insulators but poor conductors of heat, which limits their use in power electronics. We disperse hexagonal boron nitride platelets in a bisphenol-A epoxy at volume fractions from 0 to 30% and measure the thermal conductivity at 25 °C with a transient hot-wire probe. The conductivity rises from 0.20 W/(m K) for the neat resin to 0.44 W/(m K) at 30 vol%, a factor of 2.2. A Maxwell effective-medium model describes all compositions with a single filler conductivity of about 10 W/(m K), far below the bulk value, pointing to interfacial resistance as the limiting factor.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Keywords: </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>thermal conductivity · epoxy composites · boron nitride · effective-medium theory</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Introduction</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Heat removal is a central constraint in compact power electronics, where a polymer encapsulant must insulate electrically yet carry heat away from the device. Neat epoxies conduct only about 0.2 W/(m K), two to three orders of magnitude less than ceramics. The usual remedy is to load the resin with a ceramic filler, and hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) is attractive because it combines a high in-plane conductivity with electrical resistivity above 10</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:vertAlign w:val="superscript"/></w:rPr><w:t>12</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> Ω cm </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1, 2]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Reported gains vary widely between laboratories, partly because the measurement method, the platelet size and the filler–matrix interface differ from study to study. Here we prepare a single series of composites from one resin batch and one filler grade, measure them with one method, and test whether a simple effective-medium model can describe the whole series. Section </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>2</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> describes the samples and the measurement, Section </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>3</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> gives the results, and Section </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>4</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> discusses them.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Materials and methods</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2.1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Sample preparation</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Composites were made in five steps:</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The filler (h-BN platelets, median lateral size 5 µm) was dried for 12 h at 120 °C.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The resin and hardener were mixed at the stoichiometric ratio and degassed for 10 min.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The filler was added in portions and homogenised in a planetary mixer at 2000 rpm.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The mixture was cast into cylindrical moulds 40 mm in diameter and 80 mm tall.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Samples were cured for 2 h at 80 °C and 4 h at 120 °C.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Six compositions were prepared, from 0 to 30 vol% filler. Author¹, B. Coauthor¹, C. Reviewer²</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:vertAlign w:val="superscript"/></w:rPr><w:footnoteReference w:id="1"/></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="center"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>¹ Department of Materials Engineering, Northfield University</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="center"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>² Halden Institute of Applied Physics</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="center"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:i w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t>a.author@example.org</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>Epoxy resins are good electrical insulators but poor conductors of heat, which limits their use in power electronics. We disperse hexagonal boron nitride platelets in a bisphenol-A epoxy at volume fractions from 0 to 30% and measure the thermal conductivity at 25 °C with a transient hot-wire probe. The conductivity rises from 0.20 W/(m K) for the neat resin to 0.44 W/(m K) at 30 vol%, a factor of 2.2. A Maxwell effective-medium model describes all compositions with a single filler conductivity of about 10 W/(m K), far below the bulk value, pointing to interfacial resistance as the limiting factor.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Keywords: </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>thermal conductivity · epoxy composites · boron nitride · effective-medium theory</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Introduction</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Heat removal is a central constraint in compact power electronics, where a polymer encapsulant must insulate electrically yet carry heat away from the device. Neat epoxies conduct only about 0.2 W/(m K), two to three orders of magnitude less than ceramics. The usual remedy is to load the resin with a ceramic filler, and hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) is attractive because it combines a high in-plane conductivity with electrical resistivity above 10</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:vertAlign w:val="superscript"/></w:rPr><w:t>12</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> Ω cm </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1, 2]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Reported gains vary widely between laboratories, partly because the measurement method, the platelet size and the filler–matrix interface differ from study to study. Here we prepare a single series of composites from one resin batch and one filler grade, measure them with one method, and test whether a simple effective-medium model can describe the whole series. Section </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>2</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> describes the samples and the measurement, Section </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>3</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> gives the results, and Section </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>4</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> discusses them.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Materials and methods</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2.1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Sample preparation</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Composites were made in five steps:</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The filler (h-BN platelets, median lateral size 5 µm) was dried for 12 h at 120 °C.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The resin and hardener were mixed at the stoichiometric ratio and degassed for 10 min.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The filler was added in portions and homogenised in a planetary mixer at 2000 rpm.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The mixture was cast into cylindrical moulds 40 mm in diameter and 80 mm tall.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Samples were cured for 2 h at 80 °C and 4 h at 120 °C.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Six compositions were prepared, from 0 to 30 vol% filler. This is expected for randomly oriented platelets separated from the matrix by an interfacial thermal resistance, and it is consistent with other epoxy–ceramic composites </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[2, 3]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. Because Eq. </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>(2)</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> is insensitive to </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:e><m:r><m:t>k</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:t>f</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> above about 30 W/(m K), the data cannot tell a poor interface from a poor filler; direct interface or single-platelet measurements would be needed.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Two limitations should be kept in mind. And all samples came from one resin batch, so batch-to-batch variation is not included in the uncertainties.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">5 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Conclusions</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Adding 30 vol% h-BN raises the thermal conductivity of an epoxy resin from 0.20 to 0.44 W/(m K). <w:document xmlns:wpc="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingCanvas" xmlns:mo="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/mac/office/2008/main" xmlns:mc="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/markup-compatibility/2006" xmlns:mv="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:mac:vml" xmlns:o="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:office" xmlns:r="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships" xmlns:m="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/math" xmlns:v="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:vml" xmlns:wp14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:wp="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:w10="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:word" xmlns:w="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/wordprocessingml/2006/main" xmlns:w14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordml" xmlns:wpg="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingGroup" xmlns:wpi="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingInk" xmlns:wne="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2006/wordml" xmlns:wps="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingShape" mc:Ignorable="w14 wp14"><w:body><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Title"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Thermal conductivity of boron nitride–epoxy composites</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Subtitle"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>A. Author</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Subtitle"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>B. Coauthor</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Subtitle"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>C. Reviewer</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:vertAlign w:val="superscript"/></w:rPr><w:footnoteReference w:id="1"/></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="center"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:i w:val="0"/></w:rPr><w:t>a.author@example.org</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>Epoxy resins are good electrical insulators but poor conductors of heat, which limits their use in power electronics. We disperse hexagonal boron nitride platelets in a bisphenol-A epoxy at volume fractions from 0 to 30% and measure the thermal conductivity at 25 °C with a transient hot-wire probe. The conductivity rises from 0.20 W/(m K) for the neat resin to 0.44 W/(m K) at 30 vol%, a factor of 2.2. A Maxwell effective-medium model describes all compositions with a single filler conductivity of about 10 W/(m K), far below the bulk value, pointing to interfacial resistance as the limiting factor.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Keywords: </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>thermal conductivity · epoxy composites · boron nitride · effective-medium theory</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Introduction</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Heat removal is a central constraint in compact power electronics, where a polymer encapsulant must insulate electrically yet carry heat away from the device. Neat epoxies conduct only about 0.2 W/(m K), two to three orders of magnitude less than ceramics. The usual remedy is to load the resin with a ceramic filler, and hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) is attractive because it combines a high in-plane conductivity with electrical resistivity above 10</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:vertAlign w:val="superscript"/></w:rPr><w:t>12</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> Ω cm </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1, 2]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Reported gains vary widely between laboratories, partly because the measurement method, the platelet size and the filler–matrix interface differ from study to study. Here we prepare a single series of composites from one resin batch and one filler grade, measure them with one method, and test whether a simple effective-medium model can describe the whole series. Researcher — Materials Science, Somewhere</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>This review surveys machine-learning methods for the discovery of inorganic crystalline materials, in work published between 2016 and 2026. We organise the literature into three themes (property prediction, generative design and active learning), compare representative methods and their reported accuracy, and identify four open challenges: scarce experimental data, uncertainty quantification, multi-objective design and reproducibility.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Keywords: </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>machine learning · materials discovery · graph neural networks · generative models · active learning</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Introduction</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Finding a material with a target combination of properties is a search problem over an enormous space of compositions and structures. Early statistical models mapped hand-built descriptors to properties </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>(varga2016?; lindqvist2018?)</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">; the field has since added generative models that propose new compounds </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>(okafor2019?; brandt2021?)</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> and active-learning loops that choose the next experiment </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>(moreau2020?)</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. The review is restricted to inorganic crystals; molecular and polymer systems are surveyed elsewhere </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>(haddad2022?)</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Section </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>2</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> covers property prediction, Section </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>3</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> generative design and Section </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>4</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> active learning. Variational autoencoders were applied first </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>(okafor2019?)</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, followed by adversarial networks and, more recently, diffusion models </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>(brandt2021?)</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. The central difficulty is synthesisability. </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>brandt2021?</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> conditioned generation on distance to the convex hull of formation energies, so that proposed compounds are close to thermodynamic stability.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">4 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Active learning</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Active learning closes the loop between model and laboratory by selecting the measurement with the highest expected information gain. </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>moreau2020?</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> used a Gaussian-process surrogate to find a target alloy composition with three times fewer experiments than a grid search. <w:document xmlns:wpc="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingCanvas" xmlns:mo="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/mac/office/2008/main" xmlns:mc="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/markup-compatibility/2006" xmlns:mv="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:mac:vml" xmlns:o="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:office" xmlns:r="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships" xmlns:m="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/math" xmlns:v="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:vml" xmlns:wp14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:wp="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:w10="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:word" xmlns:w="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/wordprocessingml/2006/main" xmlns:w14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordml" xmlns:wpg="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingGroup" xmlns:wpi="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingInk" xmlns:wne="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2006/wordml" xmlns:wps="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingShape" mc:Ignorable="w14 wp14"><w:body><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Title"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Calibration of a low-cost capacitive soil-moisture probe across three soil textures</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Subtitle"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Priya Raman, Tomas Lindqvist, Amara Okafor</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>Low-cost capacitive probes make dense soil-moisture networks affordable, but their output depends on soil texture and temperature. We calibrated 12 probes against oven-dry gravimetric measurements in a sand, a loam and a clay soil (144 samples in total). A quadratic relation between probe voltage and volumetric water content gave root-mean-square errors (RMSE) of 0.012, 0.015 and 0.021 m³ m⁻³ for the three soils, and 0.019 m³ m⁻³ for a single pooled model. Between 278 and 293 K the temperature drift stayed below 0.004 m³ m⁻³. Texture-specific calibration is therefore advisable when the error budget is below 0.02 m³ m⁻³.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Keywords: </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>soil moisture · capacitive sensor · calibration · low-cost instrumentation · precision agriculture</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Courier New" w:hAnsi="Courier New"/></w:rPr><w:t>\linenumbers</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Introduction</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Irrigation scheduling needs soil-moisture data at the scale of a field, which means tens or hundreds of probes rather than one. Commercial time-domain reflectometry probes cost several hundred dollars each, while capacitive probes built around a 555 timer cost about 3 USD; their price has opened the door to dense networks </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1, 2]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. The cost is paid in accuracy: the factory calibration is a straight line between air and water, and the probes respond to soil bulk density, salinity and temperature as well as to water </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[2]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">This paper answers a practical question: how much is gained by calibrating for each soil texture, compared with a single calibration for all soils? We describe the calibration procedure (Section </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>2</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">), report the errors for three contrasting soils (Section </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>3</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">) and discuss the temperature effect and the limits of the approach (Section </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>4</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>).</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Materials and methods</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2.1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Probe and soils</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Twelve identical probes were read with a 12-bit analogue-to-digital converter at 3.3 V. Three soils were sampled from the top 20 cm of experimental plots: a sand (92% sand), a loam (41% sand, 38% silt) and a clay (58% clay). Each soil was air-dried, sieved to 2 mm and packed to a bulk density of 1.35 g cm⁻³ in 1 L cylinders.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2.2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Calibration procedure</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Each cylinder was wetted to eight water contents between air-dry and saturation and equilibrated for 24 h. The probe voltage </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>V</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> was recorded for 5 min, after which a 20 mL core was weighed wet and oven-dried at 105 °C to obtain the volumetric water content </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>θ</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t>. We fitted the quadratic model</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><m:oMathPara><m:oMath><m:eqArr><m:e><m:r><m:t>θ=</m:t></m:r><m:sSub><m:e><m:r><m:t>a</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:t>0</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub><m:r><m:t>+</m:t></m:r><m:sSub><m:e><m:r><m:t>a</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:t>1</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub><m:r><m:t>V+</m:t></m:r><m:sSub><m:e><m:r><m:t>a</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:t>2</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub><m:sSup><m:e><m:r><m:t>V</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sup><m:r><m:t>2</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSup><m:r><m:t>#(1)</m:t></m:r></m:e></m:eqArr></m:oMath></m:oMathPara></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">by least squares, either separately for each soil or for all 144 samples together. Goodness of fit is reported as the coefficient of determination </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSup><m:e><m:r><m:t>R</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sup><m:r><m:t>2</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSup></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> and the RMSE of </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>(2)</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>:</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><m:oMathPara><m:oMath><m:eqArr><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><m:t>RMSE</m:t></m:r><m:r><m:t>=</m:t></m:r><m:rad><m:radPr><m:degHide m:val="1"/></m:radPr><m:deg/><m:e><m:f><m:num><m:r><m:t>1</m:t></m:r></m:num><m:den><m:r><m:t>n</m:t></m:r></m:den></m:f><m:nary><m:naryPr><m:chr m:val="∑"/></m:naryPr><m:sub><m:r><m:t>i=1</m:t></m:r></m:sub><m:sup><m:r><m:t>n</m:t></m:r></m:sup><m:e><m:sSup><m:e><m:d><m:dPr><m:begChr m:val="("/><m:endChr m:val=")"/></m:dPr><m:e><m:sSubSup><m:e><m:r><m:t>θ</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:t>i</m:t></m:r></m:sub><m:sup><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><m:t>model</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSubSup><m:r><m:t>−</m:t></m:r><m:sSubSup><m:e><m:r><m:t>θ</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:t>i</m:t></m:r></m:sub><m:sup><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><m:t>ref</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSubSup></m:e></m:d></m:e><m:sup><m:r><m:t>2</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSup></m:e></m:nary></m:e></m:rad><m:r><m:t>#(2)</m:t></m:r></m:e></m:eqArr></m:oMath></m:oMathPara></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Temperature drift was measured by cycling the loam cylinders between 278 and 293 K in a climate chamber at constant water content.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">3 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Results</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Table </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>1</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> lists the fit quality. E-mail: j.weber@example.edu</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>Plasterboard partitions with a cavity are the standard lightweight wall. We measured the weighted sound reduction index Rw of three configurations in a laboratory test facility and compared the results with the mass law and with the mass–air–mass resonance frequency. Doubling the board mass raised Rw by 5 dB, while a 100 mm cavity with mineral wool added a further 9 dB, reaching 45 dB. The resonance frequency of 85 Hz predicted from the cavity depth lies below the building-acoustics range, so the wall performs close to the double-leaf ideal.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Keywords: </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>sound insulation · double-leaf wall · mass law · plasterboard</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Introduction</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Lightweight partitions cover most interior walls in modern buildings. w:val="Title"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Energy-Aware Duty-Cycle Scheduling for Class A LoRaWAN Sensor Nodes</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>Battery life limits long-range wireless sensor networks, and most of the energy of a LoRaWAN node goes into transmitting. We propose a scheduler that picks the spreading factor and the reporting interval of each node from its measured collision probability. In a simulation of 500 nodes around one gateway the scheduler raised the packet delivery ratio from 78.4% to 94.2% and cut the energy per uplink by 34%, which extends the expected battery life from 2.1 to 3.2 years.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Keywords: </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>LoRaWAN · duty cycle · energy efficiency · wireless sensor networks · scheduling</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Introduction</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Low-power wide-area networks connect sensors that must run for years on a battery. In LoRaWAN, a Class A node sends an uplink whenever it has data and opens two short receive windows afterwards </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>. Because nodes share the channel by pure ALOHA, collisions grow with the number of nodes, and every lost uplink wastes the energy spent on it.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The contributions of this paper are: (i) an energy and collision model for Class A nodes; (ii) a distributed scheduler that needs no extra downlink traffic; and (iii) a simulation study with 500 nodes.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Related Work</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">The adaptive data rate (ADR) mechanism of LoRaWAN selects the spreading factor from the link margin </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. It ignores the load of the cell. Scheduling approaches that assign time slots need tight synchronisation </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[2]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>, which Class A nodes do not have. probe</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>We measure the population of a laser-driven two-level system as a function of pulse duration and detuning and compare it with the generalized Rabi formula. The Rabi frequency grows as the square root of the drive power, from 12.4 kHz at 0.5 mW to 99.3 kHz at 32 mW, and the measured π-pulse durations follow from the fit within 1%. A decay constant of 180 μs limits the contrast of the oscillations.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Keywords: </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Rabi oscillations; two-level system; coherent control; detuning</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Introduction</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Coherent driving of a two-level system is the basic operation behind atomic clocks, quantum gates and magnetic resonance </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1, 2]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>. The population of the excited state oscillates between zero and one at the Rabi frequency, and the oscillation is faster but shallower when the drive is detuned. Homogeneous catalysts are active but hard to remove from the product, which matters for pharmaceutical intermediates. Supported nanoparticles are an alternative if they stay on the support and do not leach </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[2, 1]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>. Nitrogen sites in doped carbon anchor Pd and keep the particles small.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Experimental Section</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2.1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>General</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Solvents and reagents were used as received. We describe a membership filter that stores short fingerprints in a table of small buckets, where each key may live in one of two buckets. We prove a closed-form bound on the false-positive rate, show that with 12-bit fingerprints the structure needs about 12.6 bits per key at 95% load, and report that a prototype drops 99.8% of synthetic duplicates at 2.1 million events per second on a single core.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Keywords: </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>approximate membership · hashing · stream processing</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Introduction</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">A message broker that delivers at least once must remove duplicates before an event reaches a consumer. Keeping all identifiers in a hash set costs tens of bytes per key; an approximate filter answers the question </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>have we seen this key?</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> in a few bits, at the price of a small chance of a false positive and no chance of a false negative. Bloom filters </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> are the textbook answer, but they cannot delete a key, which a sliding window over a stream requires.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Our contributions are:</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>a fingerprint filter with two candidate buckets per key and a bounded eviction walk;</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>a closed-form false-positive bound (Theorem 1) and its space cost in bits per key;</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>an evaluation on synthetic click streams showing that the filter matches a Bloom filter in space while supporting deletion.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Section </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>2</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> describes the design, Sect. </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>3</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> the analysis and Sect. </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>4</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> the evaluation. We measured nitrate-nitrogen at the inlet and outlet of three restored wetlands over one hydrological year. Annual retention was 29 to 46% of inflow concentration. A first-order removal model with a single rate constant of 0.12 to 0.14 per day reproduced all three sites, which indicates that hydraulic residence time, rather than wetland age or area, controls retention. Managing outflow to lengthen residence time in the wet season is therefore the most direct lever for improving performance.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Keywords: </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>wetland restoration · nitrate · residence time · catchment management</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Introduction</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Nitrate leaching from fertilised fields degrades downstream water quality and drives eutrophication of estuaries </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. Constructed and restored wetlands intercept drainage and remove nitrate by plant uptake and denitrification, the microbial reduction of nitrate to nitrogen gas. Reported removal ranges widely, from a few per cent to well over half of the inflowing load </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[2, 1]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>, and it is unclear which design variable explains the spread.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Here we test whether a single parameter, the hydraulic residence time </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>τ</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t>, explains retention across three restored wetlands of different age and size in one catchment.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Methods</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2.1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Study sites</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The three wetlands (A to C) drain pasture and arable fields in a 14 km</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:vertAlign w:val="superscript"/></w:rPr><w:t>2</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> catchment. They were restored 3 years (A), 7 years (B) and 11 years (C) before the study, and cover 0.8, 1.4 and 0.5 ha.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2.2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Sampling and analysis</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Inlet and outlet were sampled weekly from October to September with flow-proportional autosamplers. </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSup><m:e><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><m:t>d</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sup><m:r><m:t>−1</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSup></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, a spread of less than 20% around the mean of 0.13, although the wetlands differ threefold in area and almost fourfold in age. Retention tracks residence time: the site with the longest </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>τ</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> retained the most.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">4 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Discussion</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">The similar rate constants suggest that removal per unit time is a property of the catchment's temperature, carbon supply and flora, which the three sites share, rather than of the age of the wetland. This agrees with the view that wetland performance stabilises within a few years of restoration </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[2]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Two caveats apply. First, three sites cannot separate residence time from other site traits. Second, sampling was weekly, so short storm pulses are under-represented. Management implications are:</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>keep outlets adjustable so that residence time can be raised in the wet season;</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>design for a residence time above about 5 days, which gave 45% retention here;</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>prioritise sites with a large share of the catchment's drainage over additional area.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">5 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Conclusions</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Nitrate retention in three restored headwater wetlands followed a single first-order law in the residence time. <w:document xmlns:wpc="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingCanvas" xmlns:mo="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/mac/office/2008/main" xmlns:mc="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/markup-compatibility/2006" xmlns:mv="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:mac:vml" xmlns:o="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:office" xmlns:r="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships" xmlns:m="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/math" xmlns:v="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:vml" xmlns:wp14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:wp="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:w10="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:word" xmlns:w="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/wordprocessingml/2006/main" xmlns:w14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordml" xmlns:wpg="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingGroup" xmlns:wpi="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingInk" xmlns:wne="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2006/wordml" xmlns:wps="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingShape" mc:Ignorable="w14 wp14"><w:body><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Title"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Does Generous Line Height Help? Reading Speed and Comfort on Phone Screens</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Subtitle"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Rosa Salgado</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="center"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>University of Northfield</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Subtitle"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Idris Ketterman</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="center"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>Lowmoor Design Studio</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>Phone interfaces often set body text with tight line spacing to fit more words on screen. We ran a within-subjects study with 36 participants who read three short articles, each set with a line height of 1.2, 1.4 or 1.6 times the font size. Reading speed differed across conditions (F(2, 70) = 6.84, p = .002): the 1.4 setting was read about 5% faster than the tightest one, and participants rated it as most comfortable. Going from 1.4 to 1.6 brought no further gain. We discuss defaults for mobile reading interfaces.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Introduction</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">People read long texts on phones more than ever, yet layout defaults are tuned for screenshots rather than for reading. Line height is a cheap parameter to change: classic typographic advice favours generous leading for long lines </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, but phone lines are short, and the benefit is unclear. Prior work on small screens compared font sizes and column widths </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[2]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> rather than vertical spacing.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>We ask two questions:</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Does line height change reading speed on a phone when comprehension is held constant?</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListNumber"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Which line height do readers prefer?</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Related Work</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Studies of print typography found that very tight leading slows readers because the eye drifts to the neighbouring line </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. On screens the effect depends on line length: Lindgren and Aziz report that the optimum moves towards tighter spacing as lines get shorter </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[3]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, which is the regime of phones. Work on mobile reading has focused on how text is delivered, for example rapid serial presentation, rather than on its static layout </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[2, 4]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>. We complement it with a controlled test of one layout parameter.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">3 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Method</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">3.1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Participants and design</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>We recruited 36 adults (20 women, 15 men, 1 not disclosed; ages 19 to 58, median 31) through a university mailing list. All read English as a first language and had normal or corrected vision. Each participant read three articles of about 450 words (Flesch reading ease 62 to 66) in one of the three line heights. Condition order and article assignment were counterbalanced with a Latin square.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">3.2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Apparatus and procedure</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Texts were shown in a web page on a 6.1-inch phone at a 16 px serif font, with 32-character lines. Participants scrolled at their own pace; scroll events gave the reading time. After each article they answered four multiple-choice questions and rated comfort on a seven-point scale. Reading speed is words divided by reading time, </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>v=</m:t></m:r><m:f><m:num><m:r><m:t>N</m:t></m:r></m:num><m:den><m:r><m:t>t</m:t></m:r></m:den></m:f><m:r><m:t>⋅60</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t>, in words per minute (wpm).</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>We analysed speed only for articles on which at least three of the four questions were answered correctly, which excluded 7 of 108 readings. The omnibus test was followed by paired comparisons with a Holm correction.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">4 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Results</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Comprehension was high and did not differ between conditions (about 3.4 of 4 questions in each). Mean reading speed is shown in Table </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>1</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. Comfort followed the same order, and when asked to pick a favourite, 22 participants chose 1.4, 9 chose 1.6 and 5 chose 1.2.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Reading speed and comfort were only weakly related (Pearson </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>r=.21</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t>), so the preference for 1.4 is not simply a matter of reading faster.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">5 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Discussion</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Our results support a modest increase over the tightest common setting. The gain is small in absolute terms, about 12 wpm, but it comes at the cost of roughly 15% more vertical space and is free of any other interface change. We caution against extrapolating beyond short articles, 16 px type and 32-character lines; larger studies should vary these jointly. Our participants were also young and mostly university affiliated, and the three articles, although matched on length and difficulty, are a small sample of text.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Design implications are straightforward:</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>default to a line height near 1.4 for body text on phones;</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>do not trade readability for density by going below 1.2;</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>offer the setting to readers with low vision, who were not part of our sample.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">6 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Conclusion</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>In a controlled study, a line height of 1.4 gave faster and more comfortable phone reading than 1.2, and 1.6 added nothing. We hope these numbers help practitioners set defensible defaults.</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:vertAlign w:val="superscript"/></w:rPr><w:footnoteReference w:id="1"/></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>References</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:ind w:left="567" w:hanging="567"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>[1]</w:t><w:tab/></w:r><w:r><w:t>Brandt, K. 2012. <w:document xmlns:wpc="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingCanvas" xmlns:mo="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/mac/office/2008/main" xmlns:mc="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/markup-compatibility/2006" xmlns:mv="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:mac:vml" xmlns:o="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:office" xmlns:r="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships" xmlns:m="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/math" xmlns:v="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:vml" xmlns:wp14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:wp="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:w10="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:word" xmlns:w="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/wordprocessingml/2006/main" xmlns:w14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordml" xmlns:wpg="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingGroup" xmlns:wpi="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingInk" xmlns:wne="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2006/wordml" xmlns:wps="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingShape" mc:Ignorable="w14 wp14"><w:body><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Title"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Ten Minutes of Expressive Writing Before an Exam Reduces Test Anxiety in First-Year Students</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>Test anxiety impairs the performance of many students. Expressive writing about worries has been proposed as a brief intervention, but evidence from classroom settings is limited. In a randomized experiment, 96 first-year psychology students wrote for 10 min about their thoughts and feelings about an upcoming exam or about their morning routine. Students in the expressive writing condition reported lower test anxiety immediately before the exam than controls, with a medium effect. Exam scores were higher in the writing group, but the difference was not statistically significant. The results support short writing tasks as a low-cost way to reduce anxiety before assessments.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:b/></w:rPr><w:t xml:space="preserve">Keywords: </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>test anxiety · expressive writing · randomized experiment · higher education</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Test anxiety, the tendency to worry about evaluation and to feel tense before and during exams, is common among students and is associated with lower exam performance </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>(calder16?)</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">. Anxious students devote part of their working memory to worry, which leaves less capacity for the task itself </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>(nwosu18?)</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Expressive writing, in which people write about their deepest thoughts and feelings, offers a brief way to offload that worry. </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>nwosu18?</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> asked students to write before an exam and found better scores, but their sample came from a laboratory rather than a classroom. The present study tests the effect on anxiety and performance in a real course. We predicted that students who wrote about their exam worries would report less anxiety (Hypothesis 1) and obtain higher scores (Hypothesis 2) than students in a control condition.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Method</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Participants</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Participants were 96 first-year students (</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>M</w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:e/><m:sub><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><m:t>age</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> = 19.2 years, </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>SD</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> = 1.4; 71% women) enrolled in an introductory psychology course at a large public university. They took part for course credit. A power analysis for a two-tailed independent-samples </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>t</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> test with </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>d</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> = 0.5, </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>α=.05</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> and power of .80 gave a target of about 64 participants per group, so we enrolled 48 per group, as many as the course could provide, and accept a reduced power of about .68.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Materials and procedure</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Ten minutes before their first midterm, students were randomly assigned to one of two conditions. In the </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>expressive writing</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> condition they wrote about their thoughts and feelings about the exam; in the </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>control</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> condition they described their morning routine. Immediately afterward they completed the Test Anxiety Inventory, a 20-item scale with scores from 20 to 80. Higher scores mean more anxiety (Cronbach's </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>α=.91</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> in this sample). The exam score was the percentage correct on the 60-item multiple-choice midterm.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Analysis</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Conditions were compared with independent-samples </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>t</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> tests. Student</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="center"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>Department of Computer Science, University of Somewhere</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>Sparse linear models are a workhorse of data analysis, but fitting them on datasets with millions of features remains slow. <w:document xmlns:wpc="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingCanvas" xmlns:mo="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/mac/office/2008/main" xmlns:mc="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/markup-compatibility/2006" xmlns:mv="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:mac:vml" xmlns:o="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:office" xmlns:r="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships" xmlns:m="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/math" xmlns:v="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:vml" xmlns:wp14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:wp="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:w10="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:word" xmlns:w="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/wordprocessingml/2006/main" xmlns:w14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordml" xmlns:wpg="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingGroup" xmlns:wpi="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingInk" xmlns:wne="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2006/wordml" xmlns:wps="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingShape" mc:Ignorable="w14 wp14"><w:body><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Title"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The Living Estuary</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Subtitle"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Marguerite Aldous</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Where the River Gives Up</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>An estuary is a place of argument. Twice a day the sea pushes inland, and twice a day the river pushes back; everything that lives between the two has to cope with water that changes its mind. Walk the mud of the Wenlow Estuary at low tide and you stand on the floor of a sea that left an hour ago and will return before supper.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>This book follows one such estuary through a single year. It is not a field manual, although it borrows from several; it is closer to a long walk with a good companion who stops often to point at things. The first chapter explains the physical machine, the tide and the salt gradient it drives. The second looks at the animals that have made a living inside that machine.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1.1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>The tidal machine</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The Wenlow rises on peat moorland and runs forty kilometres to the sea, but its last twelve kilometres belong to the tide. At spring tides the water at the mouth rises and falls by 5.8 metres; at the head of the estuary, where the channel narrows and the bed shoals, the range is larger still, an effect known as funnelling</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:vertAlign w:val="superscript"/></w:rPr><w:footnoteReference w:id="1"/></w:r><w:r><w:t>. Hydrographers estimate the volume of water that enters and leaves on each tide with the tidal prism,</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><m:oMathPara><m:oMath><m:eqArr><m:e><m:r><m:t>P=</m:t></m:r><m:sSub><m:e><m:r><m:t>A</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><m:t>s</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub><m:r><m:t xml:space="preserve"> R,</m:t></m:r><m:r><m:t>#(1)</m:t></m:r></m:e></m:eqArr></m:oMath></m:oMathPara></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">where </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:e><m:r><m:t>A</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><m:t>s</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> is the surface area of the estuary at mid-tide and </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>R</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> is the tidal range. For the Wenlow, </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:e><m:r><m:t>A</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:rPr><m:sty m:val="p"/></m:rPr><m:t>s</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub><m:r><m:t>=14.2</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> km</w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSup><m:e/><m:sup><m:r><m:t>2</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSup></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> and </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>R=4.1</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> m on an average tide, so Equation </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>1</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> gives a prism of roughly </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>5.8×1</m:t></m:r><m:sSup><m:e><m:r><m:t>0</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sup><m:r><m:t>7</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSup></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> cubic metres. That is about two hundred times the volume the river alone delivers over the same six hours, which is why the estuary belongs more to the sea than to the river that named it.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1.2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Salt and mud</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Salinity falls steadily from the sea to the head of the estuary, but the transition is never tidy. On a falling tide, fresher water rides over saltier water like oil on vinegar; on a spring flood the two mix violently. Biologists therefore divide an estuary into zones by the salinity an animal can expect to meet, not by distance from the sea. </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:i/></w:rPr><w:t>Salinity zones of the Wenlow Estuary at mean river flow.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The mud itself is a product of the same mixing. Fine clay particles carried by the river clump together when they meet salt water, sink, and settle in the quiet water behind the sandbanks. Over centuries this has built the broad flats that make the estuary so rich (</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>). A single square metre of healthy mud can hold ten thousand small worms and snails, and these in turn feed most of the estuary's birds.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Those Who Live in the Mud</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Life in the estuary is built on a simple bargain: tolerate the changes, and the food is enormous. Few species accept the terms. Those that do tend to be present in huge numbers, and the Wenlow is no exception.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2.1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Burrowers and grazers</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Three animals do most of the work on the mudflats.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The ragworm, which burrows in the mesohaline mud and surfaces to feed at high tide;</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>the mud snail, which grazes the film of algae on the surface and leaves tracks visible from the sea wall;</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>the baltic tellin, a thin pink bivalve that vacuums the mud with a long siphon.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">Their numbers are not constant. w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Every one of those animals is somebody's lunch. By October the flats fill with waders: knot, dunlin, redshank and curlew, each with a bill shaped for a different depth of mud. A curlew probes ten centimetres down for ragworm; a dunlin, with a short straight bill, picks tellins from the top two. They share the flats without much competition, a division of labour that ecologists call niche partitioning (</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1, 2]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>).</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The birds keep to the tide's timetable and not the clock's. Each feeds as the flats are uncovered, roosts on the saltmarsh at high water, and returns when the mud reappears. A winter day on the estuary therefore has two long meals and two long rests, offset by about fifty minutes from the day before.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>That daily rhythm is fragile. A walker with a dog on the flats at the wrong moment can send three hundred birds into the air, and each unplanned flight burns energy that a wader in January can ill afford</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:rPr><w:vertAlign w:val="superscript"/></w:rPr><w:footnoteReference w:id="2"/></w:r><w:r><w:t>. The simplest conservation measure in the estuary turns out to be an honest tide table pinned to the car park noticeboard.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>References</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:ind w:left="567" w:hanging="567"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>[1]</w:t><w:tab/></w:r><w:r><w:t>T. Harrow, Mud, Salt and Sediment. Fenmouth University Press, 1998.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:ind w:left="567" w:hanging="567"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>[2]</w:t><w:tab/></w:r><w:r><w:t>R. Vance and L. Okoro, Disturbance and energy budgets of wintering waders. Journal of Estuarine Birds 14 (2009), 211–226.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:sectPr w:rsidR="00FC693F" w:rsidRPr="0006063C" w:rsidSect="00034616"><w:pgSz w:w="12240" w:h="15840"/><w:pgMar w:top="1417" w:right="1701" w:bottom="1417" w:left="1701" w:header="720" w:footer="720" w:gutter="0"/><w:cols w:space="720"/><w:docGrid w:linePitch="360"/></w:sectPr></w:body></w:document>

<w:document xmlns:wpc="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingCanvas" xmlns:mo="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/mac/office/2008/main" xmlns:mc="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/markup-compatibility/2006" xmlns:mv="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:mac:vml" xmlns:o="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:office" xmlns:r="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships" xmlns:m="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/math" xmlns:v="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:vml" xmlns:wp14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:wp="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/drawingml/2006/wordprocessingDrawing" xmlns:w10="urn:schemas-microsoft-com:office:word" xmlns:w="http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/wordprocessingml/2006/main" xmlns:w14="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordml" xmlns:wpg="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingGroup" xmlns:wpi="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingInk" xmlns:wne="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2006/wordml" xmlns:wps="http://schemas.microsoft.com/office/word/2010/wordprocessingShape" mc:Ignorable="w14 wp14"><w:body><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Title"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>River Calder Catchment: Annual Water Quality Report 2025</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Subtitle"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Calder Catchment Partnership</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Summary</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>This report presents the results of the 2025 monitoring programme on the River Calder and its four main tributaries. Twenty-four sites were sampled monthly for nutrients, dissolved oxygen, and faecal indicator organisms. Overall water quality improved at nineteen sites compared with 2024. Phosphorus remains the principal concern: eleven sites exceeded the 0.05 mg/L good-status threshold, mostly downstream of sewage treatment works.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The main findings are:</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>median total phosphorus fell from 0.071 to 0.058 mg/L across the catchment;</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>dissolved oxygen met the standard at all sites in every month except July at Holme Bridge;</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="ListBullet"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>bathing-water classification at Calder Weir improved from sufficient to good.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Introduction</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1.1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Purpose and scope</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The Calder Catchment Partnership brings together the water company, three local authorities, farming groups, and volunteer anglers. Its monitoring programme gives a shared evidence base for decisions on investment and enforcement. This report covers the calendar year 2025 and follows the method of the 2023 and 2024 reports so that results can be compared directly (</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>).</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1.2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>The catchment</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>The catchment covers 412 km</w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSup><m:e/><m:sup><m:r><m:t>2</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSup></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> and supports about 180,000 people. Upland areas to the west are managed moorland; the middle valley is mixed farming; the lower reaches pass through the towns of Holme and Ashby before meeting the estuary at Calder Weir. Mean annual rainfall is 1150 mm in the uplands and 780 mm on the coast.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Monitoring Method</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2.1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Sampling</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Grab samples were taken on the first Tuesday of each month at 24 fixed sites. Field staff measured temperature, pH, and dissolved oxygen in situ with calibrated probes. Water for laboratory analysis was kept at 4 degrees Celsius and delivered to the accredited laboratory within 24 hours.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">2.2 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Calculating nutrient load</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t>Pollutant loads were estimated from the concentration of each sample and the daily mean flow recorded at the nearest gauging station:</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><m:oMathPara><m:oMath><m:eqArr><m:e><m:r><m:t>L=k</m:t></m:r><m:nary><m:naryPr><m:chr m:val="∑"/></m:naryPr><m:sub><m:r><m:t>i=1</m:t></m:r></m:sub><m:sup><m:r><m:t>n</m:t></m:r></m:sup><m:e><m:sSub><m:e><m:r><m:t>C</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:t>i</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub><m:r><m:t xml:space="preserve"> </m:t></m:r><m:sSub><m:e><m:r><m:t>Q</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:t>i</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub><m:r><m:t>,</m:t></m:r></m:e></m:nary><m:r><m:t>#(1)</m:t></m:r></m:e></m:eqArr></m:oMath></m:oMathPara></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">where </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:e><m:r><m:t>C</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:t>i</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> is the concentration in mg/L, </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSub><m:e><m:r><m:t>Q</m:t></m:r></m:e><m:sub><m:r><m:t>i</m:t></m:r></m:sub></m:sSub></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> the flow in m</w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:sSup><m:e/><m:sup><m:r><m:t>3</m:t></m:r></m:sup></m:sSup></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">/s on the day of sample </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>i</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">, and </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>k</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> a conversion constant to kilograms per year. This thesis studies a Bose-Einstein condensate of 87Rb loaded into a ring-shaped optical lattice with 24 sites, and asks how long a quantized circulation survives when the lattice depth is raised. We derive a Bose-Hubbard description of the ring, measure the decay of the winding number with time, and find lifetimes that grow from 0.4 s to 5.2 s as the depth goes from 2 to 10 recoil energies. The decay is explained by thermally activated phase slips across the weakest link of the ring.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:r><w:rPr><w:rFonts w:ascii="Courier New" w:hAnsi="Courier New"/></w:rPr><w:t>\tableofcontents</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading1"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Introduction</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:pStyle w:val="Heading2"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">1.1 </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>Why rings?</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">A superfluid in a ring can carry a flow that never stops. Whereas a stirred cup of water comes to rest within seconds, the wave function of a condensate must return to itself after one trip around the ring, so the circulation is quantized in units of </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>ℏ/m</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> per unit radius. Such persistent currents have been observed in helium and, more recently, in dilute atomic gases </w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>[1, 2]</w:t></w:r><w:r><w:t>.</w:t></w:r></w:p><w:p><w:pPr><w:jc w:val="both"/></w:pPr><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve">The ring lattice added in this work breaks the ring into </w:t></w:r><m:oMath><m:r><m:t>N=24</m:t></m:r></m:oMath><w:r><w:t xml:space="preserve"> sites.
